pairs.rationale: Genesis names Melchizedek king of Salem and priest of God Most High and records his blessing of Abram. Its preceding context describes the return after the kings were defeated; Hebrews explicitly describes Melchizedek meeting and blessing Abraham.

Genesis names the Salem king and records a tenth of all being given. Hebrews explicitly identifies Abraham as giver and interprets the names as righteousness and peace; those name interpretations are not printed in Genesis.

The later sequence connects priestly likeness to Melchizedek with an indestructible life and the priest-for-the-age testimony. This develops the continual-priest likeness without settling historical parentage or identifying Melchizedek personally with the Son.

Genesis records the tenth-of-all transaction after Melchizedek blesses Abram. Hebrews explicitly calls the giver Abraham the patriarch and describes choice spoils and the recipient's greatness, details not all stated in the selected Genesis sentence.

Numbers assigns Israel's tithes to sons of Levi in return for Tent service. Hebrews specifically describes those receiving the priestly office and collecting from Abrahamic brothers; those office and ancestry qualifications are not the wording of the selected Numbers verses.

Genesis records Melchizedek blessing Abram and the tenth-of-all transaction. Hebrews uses this episode to contrast the recipient with the Levitical line and to identify Abraham as the promise holder; Genesis does not state that full genealogical argument here.

The preceding verse names the blessing of the promise holder by the non-Levitical tithe recipient. The source states the lesser-and-greater principle by which that blessing is interpreted, rather than introducing a second blessing event.

The chapter contrasts mortal tithe receivers with one testified alive, then contrasts priests stopped by death with Jesus' permanent priesthood. These related contrasts develop the argument without requiring the two referents to be identical.

The following verse explains the qualified claim that Levi paid through Abraham: Levi was still in his father's loins at the meeting. The source's so-to-speak qualification remains essential; no separate attendance or payment by a living Levi is asserted.

Genesis supplies the Melchizedek-and-Abram blessing and tithe episode invoked by the source's meeting reference. Levi is not named in this Genesis passage; the ancestral participation explanation belongs to Hebrews' preceding so-to-speak argument.

Psalm 109:4 supplies the priesthood according to Melchizedek's order on which Hebrews' question turns. The Psalm states the sworn continuing priesthood; Hebrews draws the contrast with Aaron and asks about Levitical perfection.

The later passage describes setting aside the preceding commandment because the law perfected nothing and introducing a better hope. This develops the source's inference that a changed priesthood entails a change of law.
The following verse identifies the other tribe as Judah and the person as our Lord, supplying the named tribal explanation for the source's altar-service contrast.

Matthew introduces Jesus Christ's origin with a genealogical sequence naming Judah and Perez. This supplies Judah-line background; the selected opening does not make Hebrews' claim about Moses' silence concerning priests from that tribe.

The testimony about a priest for the age according to Melchizedek's order supplies the scriptural warrant for the source's other-priest likeness. The intervening verse explains the contrast in terms of indestructible life.

Romans states that the risen Christ no longer dies and death no longer rules over Him, corresponding to the indestructible-life basis described in Hebrews. Romans does not discuss priestly appointment or the fleshly commandment in this verse.

Psalm 109:4 contains the Melchizedek-order priesthood testimony. Hebrews prints for the age where the Psalm prints for ever; the source quotes the priesthood clause rather than the Psalm's complete oath sentence.

The following verse explains the weakness behind setting aside the preceding commandment: the law perfected nothing, while a better hope permits approach to God. This links the stated reason to the source's conclusion.

The later passage likewise says the law's repeatedly offered sacrifices cannot perfect those approaching. It develops the imperfection claim through sacrificial repetition, while the source also introduces the better hope for drawing near to God.

The following verse completes the contrast between priests appointed without an oath and the One addressed by the Lord's sworn priesthood declaration. The source and target are stages of one argument.

Psalm 109:4 supplies the Lord's oath and continuing priesthood. Hebrews prints will not change His mind and for the age, while the Psalm prints will not change His purpose and for ever; Hebrews omits the Melchizedek-order ending in this occurrence.

Both passages name a better covenant in relation to Jesus' priestly ministry. The source calls Him guarantor, whereas the later passage calls Him mediator and speaks of better promises; the titles are preserved as distinct.

The next verse sets the death-interrupted succession of many priests against the One who remains for the age with a permanent priesthood. It supplies the contrasting case rather than a separate death narrative.

The following therefore connects permanent priesthood and remaining for the age with saving those approaching God and always living to intercede. The link makes the source's stated permanence and its consequence explicit.

Romans likewise names Christ Jesus as risen and interceding for us, adding His place at God's right hand. Hebrews explains complete salvation for those approaching God through His always-living intercession; the formulations retain their respective emphasis.

The earlier passage names Jesus the Son of God as high priest who passed through the heavens and was tested without sin. The source describes holiness and being higher than the heavens; passed through and higher than remain distinct descriptions.

The later passage likewise contrasts daily repeated priestly sacrifices with the One's single sacrifice for sins. The source adds the own-sins-and-people distinction and explicitly identifies the once-for-all offering as Himself.

The earlier sequence connects Christ's divinely given Son and priest titles with suffering, learned obedience, and being perfected. The source summarizes the oath's appointment of a Son perfected for the age in contrast to the law's weak appointees.

distinctions: Genesis uses Abram and pronoun forms where Hebrews explicitly names Abraham as tenth giver; Genesis name interpretations are not supplied by its narrative.
Melchizedek likeness, lineage, mortality and permanent-priesthood arguments are not treated as independent historical biography or personal identity proof.
Numbers assigns tithes to sons of Levi; Hebrews specifies priestly office and Abrahamic brothers.
Psalm 109:4 native numbering and differences in age/for ever and mind/purpose wording preserved.
Guarantor and mediator, and higher than versus passed through the heavens, remain distinct.
